newsitem.title: USA: Joulwan urges $2 billion for Bosnia force. [CORRECTED 23:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Joulwan urges $2 billion for Bosnia force. [CORRECTED 23:45 GMT]

text.p: The commander of U.S. forces in Europe warned Congress on Tuesday that the fighting readiness of U.S. troops there will suffer if it does not quickly approve $2 billion for peacekeeping in Bosnia.

Army Gen. George Joulwan, who is also commander of all NATO forces in Europe, said his 100,000 U.S. troops in the region are being increasingly called on to provide rescue and other extra services at high cost after the Cold War.
"I need the ($2 billion Bosnia) supplemental by April. It will have an effect on readiness if I don't get it," he said in testimony to the Senate Armed Services Committee.

The Pentagon has asked Congress to approve the special appropriation as part of the expected cost of $6.5 billion (corrects from $9.5 billion) to maintain some 8,000 U.S. troops in Bosnia through mid-1998 in a NATO-led peacekeeping force of 31,000.
Congressional appropriations committees are expected to take up the $2 billion request early next month.

Joulwan said the tempo of operations by U.S. forces in Europe, the Near East and Africa has increased five-fold in the last seven years, including the evacuation of hundreds of Americans and other foreigners from Albania.
He said U.S. Marine helicopters had now removed 808 persons from Albania -- about half of them Americans -- in a rescue operation that began last Thursday.
The Defence Department said the total included 20 persons evacuated on Monday, but no Americans were now awaiting removal from that country.

Albania, Joulwan testified, was an example of the type of operation that U.S. troops in Europe are constantly prepared to perform. But he said military readiness for such tasks would suffer if Bosnia costs were paid from training funds.

"While we breathe a sigh of relief at the extremely low casualties thus far in Bosnia, we are concerned with the costs of that operation and its effects on our readiness to deploy forces elsewhere, as well as the effect it has had on the quality of life of our service personnel and their families," he added.
Joulwan appeared before the committee with the commanders of U.S. forces in the Asia-Pacific and in South Korea.

Both Adm. Joseph Prueher, commander of Pacific forces, and Army Gen. John Tilelli, who commands 37,000 U.S. troops in South Korea, told the committee that the United States must keep a close watch on unpredictable North Korea.

Tilelli said the financial collapse of North Korea along with major food shortages there had put Pyongyang in "a downward spiral". He said those troubles had done nothing to reduce the danger from North Korea's large military force.

Prueher said that the 100,000 U.S. troops in the Asia-Pacific region was the number currently needed to maintain stability in the area. Some defence analysts have said that number could be cut in coming years because of shrinking U.S. defence budgets.
